newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - Healthdyne says buyer will pay more than Invacare.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Healthdyne says buyer will pay more than Invacare.

text.p: Healthdyne Technologies Inc. said Wednesday an unnamed buyer is willing to pay more for the medical device company than the $200 million offered by hostile bidder Invacare Corp.
Marietta, Ga.-based Healthdyne, which has been battling Invacare since January, also said it has received expressions of interest from other strategic buyers and a financial buyer.
"We intend to continue discussions with these parties," Healthdyne Chairman Parker Petit said in a statement. "We will accept the best proposal as long as it reflects the true value of the company."
Healthdyne has repeately rejected overtures by Invacare, which has raised its bid three times to the current level of $15 per share.

Healthdyne did not identify the buyer that is willing to pay more than $15 per share, only describing it as a Fortune 500 company with "a strong strategic interest" in acquiring the company. It also did not say if any of the interested buyers have made an actual offer.

The announcement from Healthdyne came one week before the company's annual meeting of shareholders, at which Invacare is seeking to install its own slate of four directors in an attempt to take control of the seven-member board and complete its proposed takeover.

Invacare, based in Elyria, Ohio, denounced the announcement and said it would start selling its stake in Healthdyne as early as Thursday even while pursuing the proxy fight. By selling shares, Invacare will be able to take advantage of a run-up in the Healthdyne stock that has been generated by speculation the company would eventually be sold for more than $15 per share.

Despite the intent to sell the stock, Invacare will be entitled to vote its 600,000 Healthdyne shares at the July 30 meeting because Healthdyne had previously set a shareholder record date of July 23.

"They have had a full month after announcing their intention to 'explore alternatives' ... to negotiate and announce a sale transaction. If they were serious about selling the company, they would have announced a deal by now," Invacare Chief Executive Officer Malachi Mixon said in a news release.

"Therefore, although we had originally been prepared to await the results of the (July 30 annual) meeting, we now intend, beginning as early as tomorrow, based on market conditions, to protect our investment by selling some or all of our Healthdyne shares through market and/or private transactions," Mixon said.
Healthdyne, which previously had said the company was not for sale, last month said it would talk with interested parties about a potential transaction.
In its statement, Healthdyne did not address the timing of a potential transaction, but indicated talks would continue after the July 30 annual meeting.
"We believe we can achieve higher value for shareholders after the board is re-elected," Petit said.
Healthdyne could not be reached for further comment, but a source close to the company said Healthdyne does not feel pressured to announce a transaction before the meeting.

"The worst time to negotiate any type of transaction is when you have a finite time frame and a gun to your head. We have alternatives that we can certainly get to fruition but we want to do it on a time frame and in an environment where we control the levers and the pressure," said the source, who did not want to be identified.

Meanwhile, rumoured British buyer BOC Group Plc was knocked out of the running Wednesday when it announced plans to sell its health care business. Although BOC had declined to comment on whether it was interested in Healthdyne, Wall Street experts had cited it as a potential interested party.
Germany's Siemens AG amd Thermo Electron Corp. also have been speculated as potential bidders for Healthdyne.

Healthdyne also said its board, if re-elected, will amend the company's bylaws to permit holders of at least 25 percent of its common stock to call special shareholder meetings. It also said it would amend its shareholder rights plans, known as a "poison pill", to allow a bidder meeting certain conditions to call a special meeting of shareholders to vote on a binding resolution to redeem the rights.

Healthdyne also said that, in the event that Invacare's four nominees were elected at the meeting, its board had authorised a $1.0 million trust to be used by the company's continuing directors to pay the expenses associated with any action taken by Invacare or its nominees.
Healthdyne's stock rose as high as $18 per share on Nasdaq, but pared some gains to close at $17.125, up 26.6 cents. Invacare shares fell $1.125 to $22.875, also on Nasdaq.
Healthdyne makes home health products for sleep disorders, breathing and infant monitors. It had sales of $118 million in 1996.
Invacare makes wheelchairs, medical care beds, respiratory products and cardiovacscular equipment and had sales of $610 million in 1996.
